questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — OAuth login end-to-end for a web app [senior] (dotnet-auth, docs2/03-oauth-from-the-code.md). Scenario: you run the identity provider behind "NetLinear": a single-page app with about 200,000 users, a confidential server-side admin app, and a nightly reporting job that calls the API with no user present. Access tokens should live about 15 minutes, users should stay signed in for up to 30 days without retyping a password, and the API must authorize by permission. Design the flows each client uses, the tokens and what the API checks, where every secret lives, and how the API verifies tokens, before you look. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] One flow per kind of client, allowed per client: authorization code with PKCE for apps acting for a user (the SPA and the admin web app), client credentials for the nightly job (machine-to-machine, no user), and the refresh grant to extend a session without a new login.
[w2] Clients configure themselves from one discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) rather than hard-coded endpoint URLs.
keyPoints.quote: which is how off-the-shelf OAuth libraries configure themselves against any provider

keyPoints.text: [w3] The authorize step is bound to the provider's own signed-in browser session, with its login and consent screens, so a caller can only obtain codes for themselves; taking the user's identity from a request parameter (the repo's user_id simplification) must not ship.
keyPoints.quote: you can only mint codes for yourself, after the provider's own login + consent UI

keyPoints.text: [w2] The client owns CSRF on the redirect: it sends a random state and checks that the echoed value matches; the provider only reflects it.
keyPoints.quote: the provider just reflects it; the client must verify it matches what it sent

keyPoints.text: [w3] The code-for-token exchange is a server-side checklist run in order: the client exists and may use this grant, a confidential client's secret is verified, and the code must belong to the client redeeming it. Credit the checks themselves; naming the attack each one closes is a bonus, not required.
keyPoints.quote: code minted for client A redeemed by client B

keyPoints.text: [w2] The API authorizes from the access token's permission claims: one policy per permission string, applied to endpoints as named policies.

[w3] Where client secrets live: the SPA is registered with no secret at all (its code ships to the browser, so PKCE carries the proof instead), while confidential clients get a generated secret stored BCrypt-hashed like a password.

[w3] Every request is verified locally against the provider's published public keys (asymmetric signing, kid in the header, no call to the provider per request), and a correct design checks signature, issuer, expiry AND audience, so a token minted for some other client or API is refused; the repo validates only the first three, which is the gap to close.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same provider at 10x (about 2,000,000 users, mobile apps and several open tabs refreshing at once, a client library that retries on timeout), plus a named failure: malware exfiltrates a user's refresh token. What breaks first, and what in your design already handles it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A refresh token is a long-lived session (30 days by default), so each use retires the presented token and issues a child linked to it under one family id; that lineage is what lets a stolen copy be noticed at all.
keyPoints.quote: every use kills the presented token and issues a child

keyPoints.text: [w3] When a dead refresh token is presented again, revoke the WHOLE token family (every descendant, including the attacker's live child) and force a fresh login: the server cannot tell attacker from victim, so it ejects both, and it writes a reuse audit event worth alerting on.
keyPoints.quote: Legitimate user logs in again; attacker is ejected.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Parallel refreshes are what break single-use first: the checks run in memory and are saved later, so they hold only for requests that arrive one at a time; with several tabs refreshing at once, guard the refresh-token row with a row version or a conditional update so exactly one of two simultaneous refreshes commits.
keyPoints.quote: Replay detection assumes requests arrive one at a time.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Rotation must be one commit: mark the old token rotated and insert its child in ONE transaction, so a crash between the two writes can never leave two live tokens in one family.
keyPoints.quote: A crash in the middle leaves two live tokens in one family.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Retries trip false alarms: if a refresh response is lost and the client library retries with the token it already sent, that token is now rotated, so reuse detection revokes the family and logs a legitimate user out; at 10x that becomes mass logouts. Fix with single-flight refresh on the client and/or a short grace window that returns the same child for an immediate repeat.

[w3] Revoking refresh tokens does not recall access tokens already issued: they are verified locally until they expire, so the short access-token lifetime is the real revocation latency (about one 15-minute window per rotation for an attacker).
[w2] Kill switches already exist at two levels: a UI session is a refresh-token family, "log out that device" revokes one family, and an admin force-logout revokes everything a user holds.
keyPoints.quote: Sessions in the UI are just refresh-token families

keyPoints.text: [w1] The token endpoint is rate-limited per client IP (a fixed window, e.g. 20 a minute in this repo, with no queue); at 10x, many users behind one carrier or office NAT share that budget.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your provider design against the alternatives the document raises: self-contained JWTs versus a per-request check with the provider, what the API verifies about a token beyond its signature, where the signing key lives, how strict redirect registration is, and how long refresh tokens live. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Self-contained JWTs buy verification without a provider round-trip on every request; the cost is that an issued token cannot be recalled before it expires, which is why access tokens stay short and refresh tokens rotate.

[w3] Check what a token is for, not only that it is signed: an ID token has a sub and a valid signature, so an API that skips the token-type check accepts it as a bearer token on [Authorize]-only endpoints.
keyPoints.quote: so it is accepted as a bearer token on the

keyPoints.text: [w3] The private signing key kept as plaintext PEM in the database means database read access is enough to forge any token for any tenant; a production design moves keys to a KMS or equivalent and audits key access and rotation.

[w2] Registering every redirect URI exactly costs flexibility (no wildcard for preview hosts), but prefix and wildcard matching is a well-known source of real OAuth vulnerabilities and RFC 9700 requires exact string matching.
keyPoints.quote: Prefix/wildcard matching is a well-known source of real OAuth vulnerabilities

keyPoints.text: [w2] Refresh lifetime is a per-client setting (30 days by default, clamped to 1-365 at registration): longer means fewer logins and a longer window for a stolen token, which rotation exists to shorten.
